market_holds: Spot is about $0.46 (Yahoo daily bars, 2026-11-13 intraday at the seal). That is 92% below the 52-week high, at the 52-week low, -14.8% over 20 days and -39% below the $0.75 registered direct price of 2026-10-01. Market cap is about $56m on about 121.6m shares (424B5 dated 2026-10-01: 101.6m shares plus 20m). The option chain is unusable (ATM spread 100% of mid), so no implied move exists. The usual print move has a median of 17.2%, and 6 of the last 8 prints went down, including the last four (-22.8%, -11.7%, -29.5%, -6.0%). The FY26 guide is $100-115m (Q2 release dated 2026-08-13), which needs roughly $28-35m a quarter in H2 against $24.3m in Q2. Q2 missed consensus by about 14%. The Q3 revenue consensus I could find is a stale $25.6m. The line the stock trades on this time is not the quarter. It is the $45.58m of 1.75% converts that mature on 2026-11-15, a Sunday, so they are payable on the report day. The Nov 11 release moved the print to Nov 16 08:30 ET 'to provide material updates on the status of its convertible debt discussions'. The stock fell about 13% intraday that day. Short interest is 12.68m shares, about 10% of the post-offering count (FINRA 2026-10-30 via equibles). Holders' marks on the notes are near par: Tenor about 96 and Context about 96.5 (13F at 2026-06-30), and Context about 96.5 at 2026-09-30.
view: This print is a debt-resolution event that comes with a quarter attached. My arithmetic: cash was $12.4m at June 30. The ATM added about $1.8m after June and the offering about $13.8m net. Operating burn is about $11m a quarter. That leaves very roughly $13-20m in mid-November against $45.6m of principal due on the release day, so Veritone cannot pay at par from cash. Three things point to a negotiated deal being announced Monday rather than a default. First, the notes are concentrated: on the 13F record, Tenor ($16.96m), Context ($15.76m) and Chicago Capital ($7m) hold about 87%. Second, the company rescheduled its call onto the maturity date, which a company planning to file would not do. Third, the October offering's lock-up explicitly carves out issuing shares 'to repay, or in exchange for' these notes. The same carve-out tells me the most likely structure includes equity for noteholders at or near today's depressed price. The near-par marks say the holders expect to be made close to whole, which at a $56m market cap means heavy dilution or a new senior claim ahead of the equity. Either way it is announced together with a quarter that very likely forces a cut to a guide that needs a large H2 ramp, from a company whose last four prints all fell. Against that, the stock has already lost 65% since late September. A deal that removes default risk without much equity, or that brings in third-party money, could squeeze a 10% short base hard. Net, I lean slightly down, with a very wide spread of outcomes and no edge I can defend.

recommendation.reason: The outcome turns on the terms of a convertible restructuring that are not public until the release. The evidence points both ways: concentrated, near-par holders and a lock-up carve-out for note-for-equity exchanges suggest dilution, but a stock already down 65% with 10% short interest could rally on any deal that removes default risk. I cannot show that the price is wrong in either direction with 65% confidence.
recommendation.what_would_flip_it: A clean refinancing (new third-party term debt or an asset sale funding a par cash paydown, with maturity extended and little or no equity to noteholders) would make this a relief squeeze up. A forbearance-only update or a missed payment would make it a large drop.

self_critique: The strongest case for up: the stock has lost about 65% in seven weeks and sits at a market cap barely above the note principal, so default is substantially priced. A rescheduled call on the maturity date is what a company does when it has a signed deal it wants to present. Concentrated holders sign fast, and distressed small caps often gap up when a maturity wall is removed, especially with about 10% short interest. If the deal is mostly new notes with an extended maturity and little equity, a 20-40% squeeze is plausible. That case is real, and it is why I stay near 50 and make no call.
approach_notes: P6 ('find the line first') was the most useful part. The line here is the maturity, not the quarter, and the 13F marks of the noteholders were a stakeholder source the P3 list pointed toward. P7's 65% bar correctly kept me out of a binary I cannot see into.
